title: HELA: Hyper-Efficient Lightweight Architecture for Image Fine-Tuning
abstract: The "pretraining + fine-tuning" paradigm currently dominates model applications. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA offer the advantage of fewer tunable parameters compared to traditional full-tuning, but they do not demonstrate significant improvements in memory consumption. Memory-efficient fine-tuning (MEFT) approaches like LST reducing memory usage while sacrificing some accuracy. We propose a novel MEFT architecture named Hela, which integrates the advantages of low tunable parameter count, low memory consumption, and high accuracy. Meanwhile, its internal modules allow flexible replacement to adapt to the latest technological advancements, enabling potential performance upgrades. Image classification experiments on 12 common datasets show that Hela outperforms all mainstream PEFT and MEFT methods. Validation across pretrained weights obtained via three different training strategies demonstrates that Hela achieves excellent and stable performance, highlighting its strong generalization ability. The code is on https://github.com/CaiX9527/Hela.

title: Soft Super-Pixel Partitioning for Certified Adversarial Robustness
abstract: Deep neural network classifiers require robustness certificates to ensure reliable predictions against adversarial perturbations. Randomized smoothing with Gaussian noise provides such guarantees, but on high-dimensional image datasets the certified radius could be limited: increasing the noise variance to enlarge the potential radius would reduce classifier confidence by degrading input visibility. To mitigate this trade-off, we propose Pixel Partitioning-based Randomized Smoothing (PPRS), a training-free method that groups pixels into partitions and averages within groups to preserve semantic structure while reducing effective noise variance. To address the instability of hard partitions under Gaussian perturbations, we further introduce a soft superpixel variant of PPRS, where smooth, row-stochastic memberships replace hard assignments and yield weighted regional averaging. This soft partitioning stabilizes boundary pixels, enhances confidence under noise, and consistently enlarges certified radii. Experiments on standard vision benchmarks and neural architectures demonstrate that PPRS with soft superpixels achieves considerable improvements in certified accuracy and robustness over the conventional randomized smoothing.

title: One-Shot Sequential Federated Learning with Dual-Distillation
abstract: One-shot Federated Learning (OFL) significantly reduces communication costs in Federated Learning (FL) by limiting the training process to a single round. Existing OFL approaches primarily adopt parallel frameworks. In contrast, Sequential FL (SFL), as an emerging FL paradigm, offers better communication efficiency compared to traditional parallel schemes. However, data heterogeneity remains a substantial challenge for both OFL and SFL due to the limited communication among clients. In this paper, we propose SFed3, a novel one-shot SFL framework with a dual-distillation method. SFed3enhances model performance under heterogeneous data by integrating personalized data distillation with model distillation. Moreover, we introduce a data pruning mechanism that filters out drifted synthetic data to prevent performance degradation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SFed3outperforms state-of-the-art OFL methods.

title: Efficient Synthetic Data Selection via Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle
abstract: Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) has emerged as a promising paradigm to leverage private data for training modern AI models while mitigating privacy concerns. However, deploying SDG in distributed and resource-constrained environments raises two challenges: (1) ensuring that transmitted synthetic data remains useful for downstream tasks, and (2) reducing the transmission overhead from the large volume of generated data. To address these issues, we formulate generative data utilization as a data selection problem that jointly minimizes utility loss and efficiency loss. The main difficulty lies in its combinatorial nature: selecting a subset of M generated samples corresponds to a binary vector γ ∈ {0, 1}M, leading to an exponential search space of size 2M. Since evaluating each candidate γ requires training a downstream model, the problem is NP-hard and infeasible by brute force. To overcome this, we reformulate the task as an optimal control problem and design a solution based on Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle (PMP), which provides an efficient approximation of the optimal selection strategy. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that our method reduces transmission volume while preserving the utility of synthetic data for downstream tasks, underscoring its potential for real-world deployment in distributed signal processing systems.

title: Anti-Exception Action Generation For Automatic Planning
abstract: We study Automatic Plan Generation (APG), a task of generating the programatically-executable plan given the objective. Large Language Models (LLMs) have been applied for APG, showing considerable potentials. However, they fail to tackle the abrupt exception that prevents the implementation of the plan. To address this issue, we propose an anti-exception action generation approach. It conducts troubleshooting by generating the exception-handled action. In particular, to relieve the aimless action generation problem, we design a reverse engineering based generation framework. This framework comprises the components of 1) priori-exception generation over source actions, 2) exception matching for optional action exploration, and 3) option-aware anti-exception action generation. We experiment on Medusa-α and Perseus-2, which are two datasets built for the research of exception-tolerated and anti-exception planning, respectively. The test results demonstrate that our approach substantially improves the anti-exception planning abilities of LLMs.

title: Stochastic Shadow Descent: Training Parametrized Quantum Circuits with Shadows of Gradients
abstract: In this paper, we focus on the task of optimizing the parameters in Parametrized Quantum Circuits (PQCs). While popular algorithms, such as Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation (SPSA), limit the number of circuit-execution to two per iteration, irrespective of the number of parameters in the circuit, they have their own challenges. These methods use central-differences to calculate biased estimates of directional derivatives. We show, both theoretically and numerically, that this may lead to instabilities in training the PQCs. To remedy this, we propose Stochastic Shadow Descent (SSD), which uses random-projections (or shadows) of the gradient to update the parameters iteratively. We eliminate the bias in directional derivatives by employing the Parameter-Shift Rule, along with techniques from Quantum Signal Processing, to construct a quantum circuit that parsimoniously computes unbiased estimates of directional derivatives. Finally, we prove the convergence of the SSD algorithm, provide worst-case bounds on the number of iterations, and numerically demonstrate its efficacy.

title: Marker-Based Instrumentation for Observing Internal Representations in Neural Language Models
abstract: Contemporary interpretability research in large language models operates predominantly through post-hoc analysis: probing trained models, tracing activations, and reverse-engineering internal representations after training is complete. This paper proposes a fundamentally different approach. Rather than forensic analysis of trained systems, we introduce the concept of training-time observability through embedded dynamic markers, a framework in which structured, behaviorally inert signals are embedded within training data prior to model training, enabling researchers to trace how specific signals propagate, transform, and persist within a model's internal representations. The central contribution is a formal design framework for such markers, which we term Steganographic Provenance Markers (SPMs). A valid SPM must satisfy four properties: non-dominance over the primary learning signal, persistence across transformation layers, recoverability through post-hoc probing, and orthogonality with respect to core semantic features. We further require that SPMs occupy the null space of the training objective, present in the distributional structure of data and carrying no gradient signal, such that the model neither optimizes toward nor away from them.

title: XSOC-NIE-GUARD: A Cryptographic Mediation Architecture for AI Agent Systems, with Application to the OpenClaw Security Crisis
abstract: The rapid adoption of AI agent frameworks through late 2025 and early 2026 produced a security crisis whose exemplar is OpenClaw, an open-source framework that as of April 2026 has accumulated 138 Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures across five months of public availability, with public exposure analysis reporting over 135,000 internet-facing instances of which approximately 63 percent run without authentication. Independent analysts have converged on the conclusion that the appropriate operator stance on any unpatched or unauthenticated deployment is to assume compromise. In parallel, Franklin, Tomašev, Jacobs, Leibo, and Osindero at Google DeepMind have published a systematic taxonomy of the AI agent attack surface that classifies six categories of adversarial content targeting different stages of an agent's operational cycle. title: GENERATIVE AI FOR ENGINEERS, SCIENTISTS, AND RESEARCHERS
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence has moved from being a niche research topic to becoming a foundational technology shaping the future of engineering, science, and scholarly inquiry. Models that can generate text, code, images, molecules, designs, and simulations are no longer experimental curiosities; they are active collaborators in laboratories, design studios, data centers, and classrooms across the world. This book, Generative AI for Engineers, Scientists, and Researchers, is written to serve as a comprehensive, rigorous, and accessible guide to this rapidly evolving field. The primary aim of this book is to bridge the gap between theoretical foundations and real-world practice. While many resources focus either on mathematical depth or on high-level applications, this volume is designed to integrate both. It begins with the core principles of generative modeling, neural networks, probability, optimization, and representation learning, and gradually builds toward advanced architectures, large-scale training, evaluation, deployment, and governance. Throughout, the emphasis remains on conceptual clarity, engineering intuition, and scientific relevance. Engineers will find in these pages a systematic treatment of how generative models can be designed, trained, evaluated, optimized, and deployed in production systems. Scientists will discover how these models can accelerate hypothesis generation, simulation, materials discovery, molecular design, and data-driven experimentation. Researchers and graduate students will gain a unified view of the theoretical underpinnings, algorithmic developments, and open challenges that define the current frontier of generative AI. A distinguishing feature of this book is its interdisciplinary scope. Generative AI is not confined to computer science; it is increasingly central to physics, chemistry, biology, materials science, climate modeling, medicine, and the social sciences. Accordingly, the text presents applications and case studies from both global and Indian contexts, highlighting how generative technologies are transforming research and innovation across diverse socio-technical environments. Equally important are the ethical, legal, and societal dimensions of generative AI. As these systems become more powerful and autonomous, questions of reliability, bias, transparency, safety, governance, and human oversight grow in significance. This book treats these issues not as peripheral concerns, but as core components of responsible scientific and engineering practice. The later chapters examine deployment, monitoring, alignment, explainability, regulatory frameworks, and the long-term implications of human–AI collaboration. The structure of the book is progressive. It moves from foundational concepts and mathematical principles, through model architectures and training paradigms, to applications in engineering and science, and finally to deployment, governance, and future directions such as autonomous scientific agents and digital twins. This organization allows readers to enter at multiple levels—whether as newcomers seeking a structured introduction or as experienced practitioners looking for a coherent synthesis of the field. Ultimately, Generative AI for Engineers, Scientists, and Researchers is written with the conviction that the future of discovery and innovation will be shaped by close collaboration between human intellect and machine intelligence. The goal is not to replace human creativity and reasoning, but to amplify them—enabling deeper understanding, faster experimentation, and more informed decision-making. It is our hope that this book will equip readers with both the technical mastery and the critical perspective required to responsibly design, deploy, and advance generative AI systems in service of science, engineering, and society.

title: Curio: A Multilingual Chatbot for Career Stream Guidance in Hindi, Marathi, and English (Preprint)
abstract: This work presents Curio, a multilingual chatbot designed to provide personalized career and stream guidance to Indian students in their native languages, including Hindi, Marathi, and English. The system integrates a rule-based expert system based on Holland’s RIASEC framework with a machine translation pipeline to enable scalable multilingual interaction. Curio aims to address the significant gap in accessible career counseling, particularly for non-English-speaking students in semi-urban and rural India. The system maps user interests to educational streams and career pathways within the Indian academic context, providing structured and interpretable recommendations. This paper describes the system architecture, methodology, and a proposed evaluation framework. A pilot study is planned to assess improvements in user clarity, decision-making confidence, and satisfaction. Note: This is a preprint version of the work and has not undergone peer review.

title: Cryptographic Applications of Strongly Regular Graph Parameter Rigidity A: A Theoretical Framework, Core Difficulties, and Open Problems
abstract: Strongly regular graphs are completely characterized by a parameter set (v,k,λ,µ).The feasible parameter space is governed by a series of strict constraints, including the basic divisibility condition, the integrality condition of eigenvalues, Kreinconditions, and absolute bounds, exhibiting a highly discrete “rigidity” feature.This paper systematically explores the theoretical possibility and intrinsic difficulties of transforming this structural rigidity into a cryptographic security resource.We identify and formalize a fundamental design dilemma—the “non-interactiveparadox”: a strictly non-interactive key exchange requires the legitimate party toreconstruct the peer’s private graph from the public parameter, which directly contradicts the underlying hardness assumption of graph structure reconstruction. Toaddress this paradox, we introduce the concept of “strongly regular graph families with trapdoors” and design a single-round bidirectional weakly interactive keyexchange protocol as a theoretical exemplar. Further security analysis reveals acritical limitation: the widely studied Paley graph family reduces to the discretelogarithm problem in the quantum computing model, thus lacking post-quantum security. This finding redirects the anchor of the underlying hard problem to stronglyregular graph families over non-abelian groups, and we discuss its potential connection to the non-abelian hidden subgroup problem. The main contribution ofthis paper is not to provide an immediately deployable cryptosystem, but rather:first, to establish a new cryptographic research paradigm based on the structuralrigidity of discrete mathematics; second, to clearly identify and formalize the coretheoretical difficulties within this paradigm (the non-interactive paradox, trapdoorconstruction, quantum vulnerability boundaries); third, to propose a series of keyopen problems for subsequent research. Properties such as extremely small publickey size demonstrate the theoretical appeal of this direction, yet concrete security parameterization and trapdoor construction still require further mathematicalbreakthroughs.

title: Traces in WAN Traffic: Inferring Alarm States and User Activity from Encrypted Smart Home Traffic
abstract: Traces in WAN Traffic: Inferring Alarm States and User Activity from Encrypted Smart Home Traffic This repository contains research data for evaluating network-traffic-based classification of Philips Hue smart-home actions. The dataset provides packet-level captures for repeated light on/off commands and labeled packet-burst features for Hue security-state commands. It is intended to support reproducible experiments on IoT traffic analysis, command inference, and device-behavior fingerprinting. Short Description Research dataset of Philips Hue smart-home network traces for IoT traffic analysis. The repository contains 10,000 labeled on/off PCAP captures and labeled packet-burst features for arm/disarm security-state commands. Dataset Contents Repository/ -- armstate_labeled.csv -- Left_Spot_device_10ktrial.7z On-Off On-Off/Left_Spot_device_10ktrial.7z contains 10,000 PCAP files captured during repeated Philips Hue light-control actions for a smart-light device communicating with a Hue Bridge Pro. The archive contains 5,000 Turn_On captures and 5,000 Turn_Off captures. File names encode the trial number, timestamp, device label and action label. Arm-Disarm Arm-Disarm/armstate_labeled.csv contains 100 labeled packet-burst feature records for Hue security-state commands: arm_home: 25 records arm_away: 25 records disarm: 50 records The CSV uses the following columns: label: command class label. TO-lengths: ordered packet-length sequence for packets sent to the target device. total-t: total burst duration in seconds. IAT: mean inter-arrival time in seconds. packet-amount: number of packets in the burst. FAIR Data Statement This dataset is structured to support the FAIR principles: Findable: Files are organized by task (On-Off, Arm-Disarm) and named with explicit device/action labels. Accessible: Data is provided in commonly supported formats: PCAP for packet captures, CSV for tabular features, and 7z for compressed distribution. Users can inspect the PCAP files with tools such as Wireshark, tshark, tcpdump, or Scapy. Interoperable: Labels, timing features, packet counts, and packet-length sequences are represented using plain-text CSV fields. Packet captures use the standard PCAP format for compatibility with established network-analysis tools. Reusable: The repository documents the dataset structure, labels, feature definitions, file naming scheme, license, and provisional citation guidance. Suggested Citation If you use this dataset, cite the accompanying paper and the archived dataset release. A final citation will be added once the publication metadata and persistent dataset identifier are available. title: An Ontology-Based Framework for Semantic Representation of the Cyber Range Domain
abstract: Cyber Ranges (CRs) are complex socio-technical ecosystems, combining infrastructure resources, software services, learning mechanisms, and human-in-the-loop processes for cybersecurity training, education, and experimentation. However, their design and representation are conventionally described by diverse architectural representations and a lack of standardization, making them difficult to compare, integrate, and reason in an automated manner. This paper proposes a novel framework that uniquely integrates the structural, functional, informational, and decisional aspects of CR platforms, formalizing them into a common semantic framework. It models the architectural and learning characteristics of CRs, allowing the representation of design choices, operational processes, information resources, and capability development. The ontology is implemented using OWL 2 DL, which includes logical constraints and enables consistency checking and automated reasoning. Validation through instantiation and competency question assessment shows that the model allows for structured querying, traceability across abstraction levels, and capability-level reasoning. The findings indicate that ontology-based modeling can serve as a basis for more formalized CR configuration analysis and capability-focused evaluation of diverse CR platforms.

title: Continual Learning for Production-Level Machine Learning in Particle Accelerators
abstract: Particle accelerators operate in complex environments where data distribution can change dynamically, leading to data drifts that significantly challenge Machine Learning (ML) models. These non-stationary conditions often cause ML models to deteriorate in performance, making it difficult to maintain reliable predictions in operation. The primary sources of data drifts are changes in accelerator settings and changes in equipment performance which cannot be measured directly. To bridge this gap between ML development and long-term deployment in operational settings, we identify key areas within particle accelerators where continual learning can help mitigate drift-induced performance degradation. We will provide a practical guide on selecting the appropriate method given resource constraints and desired stability plasticity trade offs. As a concrete example, we will present a real-world use case for anomaly detection to predict errant beams at the Spallation Neutron Source accelerator, where continual learning has been employed to demonstrate stable performance on drifting data streams. We will present practical challenges, lessons learned, and the results from the deployed ML model.

title: Performance-Guided Reinforced Active Learning for Object Detection
abstract: Active learning (AL) strategies aim to train high-performance models with minimal labeling efforts, only selecting the most informative instances for annotation. Current approaches to evaluating data informativeness predominantly focus on the data’s distribution or intrinsic information content and do not directly correlate with downstream task performance, such as mean average precision (mAP) in object detection. Thus, we propose Performance-guided (i.e.mAP-guided) Reinforced Active Learning for Object Detection (MGRAL), a novel approach that leverages the concept of expected model output changes as informativeness. To address the combinatorial explosion challenge of batch sample selection and the non-differentiable correlation between model performance and selected batches, MGRAL skillfully employs a reinforcement learning-based sampling agent that optimizes selection using policy gradient with mAP improvement as reward. Moreover, to reduce the computational overhead of mAP estimation with unlabeled samples, MGRAL utilizes an unsupervised way with fast look-up tables, ensuring feasible deployment. We evaluate MGRAL’s active learning performance on detection tasks over PASCAL VOC and COCO benchmarks. Our approach demonstrates the highest AL curve with convincing visualizations, establishing a new paradigm in reinforcement learning-driven active object detection.

title: RITA: Enhancing the Region-Independence for Transferable Targeted Attacks
abstract: The transferability of targeted attacks is critical for deceiving black-box models. Existing lightweight attacks, which avoid auxiliary networks or complex processing, often suffer from limited transferability. We propose Region-Independence Targeted Attack (RITA), a simple yet effective framework to enhance targeted transferability. Inspired by R-drop, which improves model robustness by reducing dependencies among hidden units, RITA divides perturbations into two independent regions and synchronously optimizes them to increase target class confidence. A hybrid loss function further accelerates convergence and implicitly suppresses non-target classes. Experiments on an ImageNet-compatible dataset show that RITA improves the average attack success rate by 13% over state-of-the-art methods.

title: Communication-Efficient Federated Learning with Pre-Executed Gradient Descent
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a promising distributed machine learning approach. However, FL training suffers from significant communication wait time as clients must wait for server-side model aggregation. To address this bottleneck, we propose FlowFL, a communication-efficient FL framework that enables clients to continuously train local models, eliminating waiting time for global model aggregation. To handle the staleness issues from continuous training, we develop a global model aggregation strategy with pre-executed gradient descent for accelerated convergence and a communication-friendly sparse aggregation method to reduce data transmission overhead. Compared to the benchmark FedAvg and state-of-the-art work, experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves the target accuracy while reducing up to 80% of communication rounds and 30 to 256 times of communication data, ultimately improving the model accuracy by 0.4-25.7% across five different datasets and six models.

Compared to the benchmark FedAvg and state-of-the-art work, experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves the target accuracy while reducing up to 80% of communication rounds and 30 to 256 times of communication data, ultimately improving the model accuracy by 0.4-25.7% across five different datasets and six models.

title: CodEOE: A Benchmark for Jointly Extracting Cross-Document Events and Opinions From Social Media
abstract: Event extraction and opinion/sentiment analysis have been extensively studied within recent decades, but their joint research remains an under-explored area. To bridge this gap, we introduce a challenge Cross-Document Event-Opinion Extraction (CodEOE) task, which requires a model extracting event triggers and arguments as well as their associated opinions or sentiments by understanding cross-document long contexts. We manually construct a high-quality bilingual CodEOE dataset in both Chinese and English with 6,000+ event trigger-argument pairs and 4,000+ trigger-opinion-sentiment triplets. We also develop an end-to-end grid-tagging model to benchmark the task, which jointly extracts event and opinion elements. The results of our model are comparable to those of strong baselines such as large language models. This new benchmark will advance research on both information extraction and sentiment analysis, which are very important domains of NLP. Our data, code and supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/osakana373/CodEOE.

title: Optimizing Speech Language Models for Acoustic Consistency
abstract: We study speech language models that use semantic initialization and planning losses for robust and consistent generation. CAST initializes speech tokens from self-supervised features, adds a light alignment loss, and trains with thinning and auxiliary objectives for robustness and content planning. We train three models: a 0.7B speech-only model, a 1.0B speech-only model, and a 1.0B interleaved model with text and speech. Acoustic studies show that speech-only models achieve the highest consistency across speaker, gender, sentiment, room, and background factors, surpassing larger systems. Interleaving improves lexical and syntactic probes and semantic–acoustic alignment but reduces consistency. Linear probes show that initialization favors content structure while reducing prosody detail. Overall, LM-side design and training mix control the trade-off between acoustic stability and semantic grounding without changing the tokenizer or runtime architecture. A demo and model weights are available.1

title: Enhancing Dialogue-Related Speech Tasks with Generated Spoken Dialogues
abstract: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), speech language models (SLMs) have enabled more natural spoken dialogue generation. However, to make generated dialogues useful for downstream tasks, key challenges remain in ensuring consistency between text and speech as well as providing accurate utterance timestamps. Building upon the SLIDE framework, this work introduces a method for generating dual-channel spoken dialogues with aligned transcriptions and utterance timestamps, and systematically investigates their effectiveness as augmentation data. In particular, we explore how such generated dialogues can be leveraged for downstream training in a task-specific manner—either alone or in combination with real data—across automatic speech recognition, end-to-end neural diarization, voice activity detection, and overlap speech detection. Extensive experiments on the Fisher and CALLHOME corpora demonstrate that our approach yields substantial performance gains across tasks, highlighting its effectiveness and practical value for speech processing applications.

title: Optimizing the Signal-to-Noise Ratio of Contextual Information for Improved Attributed Text Generation
abstract: Attributed text generation plays a crucial role in enhancing the reliability of large language models, as it increases transparency and credibility by generating text that can be traced back to specific sources. Existing methods consist of two stages: contextual information extraction and information integration. However, these methods face significant challenges, such as hallucination propagation and insufficient context extraction, which lead to a low signal-to-noise ratio in the contextual information integrated at the final stage. In this paper, we propose a new framework called Atomic Flow (AFlow). To address hallucination propagation, we introduce a novel paradigm known as "atomic extraction with atomic filtering" for effective hallucination detection and filtering. To tackle insufficient context extraction, we aggregate inconsistencies introduced by repeated sampling to enhance the coverage of answer-related details. Experiments on three knowledge-intensive datasets demonstrate that AFlow outperforms baseline methods, increasing answer accuracy by up to 3.65% and citation quality by up to 4.33%.

title: FedPLA: Prototype-Aligned Low-Rank Adaptation for Multimodal Federated Learning
abstract: Deploying large-scale multimodal pre-trained models at the edge faces significant challenges in computational costs and privacy preservation. Existing federated learning methods struggle to address modality missing and data heterogeneity in multimodal scenarios, leading to severe representation drift. This paper proposes FedPLA, a parameter-efficient framework that optimizes multimodal federated learning through global semantic prototype alignment. The server maintains a dual-modal prototype bank to dynamically capture global semantic distributions. On the client side, features adapted via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) are anchored to a shared prototype space using the Info Noise-Contrastive Estimation (InfoNCE) loss, enabling unimodal clients to receive implicit guidance from missing modalities. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that prototype alignment significantly accelerates convergence in non-IID scenarios. Experiments on the Hateful Memes and CrisisMMD benchmarks show that FedPLA outperforms baseline methods under extreme heterogeneity and modality-missing conditions, providing an efficient solution for privacy-preserving multimodal collaborative learning.

title: Recursive State Estimation Via Approximate Modal Paths
abstract: In this paper, a method for recursively computing approximate modal paths is developed. A recursive formulation of the modal path can be obtained either by backward or forward dynamic programming. By combining both methods, a "two-filter" formula is demonstrated. Both method involves a recursion over a so-called value function, which is intractable in general. This problem is overcome by quadratic approximation of the value function in the forward dynamic programming paradigm, resulting in both a filtering and smoothing method. The merit of the approach is verified in a simulation experiments, where it is shown to be on par or better than other modern algorithms.

title: AlignCLIP: Mining and Aligning Multi-Scale Vision-Language Features For Zero-Shot Semantic Segmentation
abstract: Zero-shot semantic segmentation requires models to generalize to unseen classes without pixel-level annotations. While recent studies have used CLIP to address this task, CLIP often misses local regions and fine-grained details, leading to performance bottlenecks. To better exploit CLIP’s potential in zero-shot segmentation, we propose AlignCLIP, a one-stage framework that fuses multi-scale image context with textual features to improve segmentation. Our approach introduces Multi-scale Region Tokens (MRT) and Context-aware Semantic Alignment (CSA) modules to capture and align features across scales. Our method demonstrates a clear advantage on unseen classes, achieving mIoU improvements of 6.7 on PASCAL VOC 2012 and 1.8 on COCO Stuff 164K over the baseline, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed multi-scale alignment strategy in enhancing cross-class generalization. The code is available at https://github.com/sekirooox/AlignCLIP.

title: KAN We Make Models Simpler for Audio Deepfake Detection with Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks?
abstract: Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KANs) are a new type of neural networks that has recently attracted attention as a possible alternative to the widely used multi–layer perceptrons (MLPs), which are the core of advanced architecture such as transformer. KANs have shown promising results in detecting spoofed speech to protect speaker verification systems. In this work, we compare the performance of a KAN layer with a traditional fully connected (FC) linear layer when using high-dimensional features from wav2vec 2.0–based model. Our findings suggest that a simpler downstream design can be much more frugal with a significantly lower number of parameters while still achieving competitive results.

title: Goal-Oriented Semantic Communication for Logical Decision Making
abstract: This paper develops a principled foundation for goal-oriented semantic communication for logical decision-making. Consider a setting where autonomous agents engage in collaborative perception. In such settings, the volume of sensory data and limited bandwidth often make transmission of raw observations infeasible, requiring intelligent selection of task-relevant information. Because these scenarios are safety-critical, the selection and decision processes must also be transparent and verifiable. To address this, we propose an explainable semantic communication framework grounded in a First-Order Logic (FOL) hierarchical representation of the world. We define semantic information, entropy, relative entropy, change in entropy, and mutual information by assigning an inductive logical probability measure over semantic structures in the language. Based on these definitions, we formulate a goal-oriented semantic communication objective through semantic rate-distortion theory and, equivalently, through the semantic information bottleneck principle. In this framework, task rules are represented as goal-oriented states, defined as a layer over the world states to capture decision-relevant abstractions. The resulting principle selects evidence that is most informative about these states, aiming to transmit only those FOL clauses most critical for decision-making while preserving logical verifiability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach in a deduction-based safe path-following task within an FOL-based urban environment simulator with multiple dynamic agents.

title: RL-ABC: Reinforcement Learning for Accelerator Beamline Control
abstract: Particle accelerator beamline optimization is a high-dimensional control problem traditionally requiring significant expert intervention. We present RLABC (Reinforcement Learning for Accelerator Beamline Control), an open-source Python framework that automatically transforms standard Elegant beamline configurations into reinforcement learning environments. RLABC integrates with the widely-used Elegant beam dynamics simulation code via SDDS-based interfaces, enabling researchers to apply modern RL algorithms to beamline optimization with minimal RL-specific development. The main contribution is a general methodology for formulating beamline tuning as a Markov decision process: RLABC automatically preprocesses lattice files to insert diagnostic watch points before each tunable element, constructs a 57-dimensional state representation from beam statistics, covariance information, and aperture constraints, and provides a configurable reward function for transmission optimization. The framework supports multiple RL algorithms through Stable-Baselines3 compatibility and implements stage learning strategies for improved training efficiency. Validation on a test beamline derived from the VEPP-5 injection complex (37 control parameters across 11 quadrupoles and 4 dipoles) demonstrates that the framework successfully enables RL-based optimization, with a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient agent achieving 70.3\% particle transmission -- performance matching established methods such as differential evolution. The framework's stage learning capability allows decomposition of complex optimization problems into manageable subproblems, improving training efficiency. The complete framework, including configuration files and example notebooks, is available as open-source software to facilitate adoption and further research.

title: Graph Neural Networks in Large Scale Wireless Communication Networks: Scalability Across Random Geometric Graphs
abstract: The growing complexity of wireless systems has accelerated the move from traditional methods to learning-based solutions. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are especially well-suited here, since wireless networks can be naturally represented as graphs. A key property of GNNs is transferability: models trained on one graph often generalize to much larger graphs with little performance loss. While empirical studies have shown that GNN-based wireless policies transfer effectively, existing theoretical guarantees do not capture this phenomenon. Most works focus on dense graphs where node degrees scale with network size—an assumption that fails in wireless systems. In this work, we provide a formal theoretical foundation for transferability on Random Geometric Graphs (RGGs), a sparse and widely used model of wireless networks. We further validate our results through numerical experiments on power allocation, a fundamental resource management task.

title: Symmetrical and Reliable Early Warning Signals for Sepsis Treatment Using Offline Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Offline reinforcement learning in safety-critical healthcare settings requires reliable risk characterisation under limited data. This thesis extends the Dead-end Discovery (DeD) framework applied to the MIMIC-III sepsis cohort along two dimensions. Using Q-value thresholding with median, minimum, and cross-action variability criteria, the framework is expanded to detect guaranteed-recovery states, the theoretical mirror image of dead-ends. No such subpopulation is detected in the sepsis cohort, suggesting recovery trajectories are too heterogeneous for value-function thresholding to identify. To assess flag reliability, epistemic uncertainty is quantified via bootstrapped Deep Q-Network ensembles, and action-conditioned data support is measured using K-nearest neighbours in the AIS latent space. Both signals are individually associated with non-survivor mortality and carry largely independent information. State-action pairs flagged as high-uncertainty under both measures show mortality rates more than seven times those flagged as low-uncertainty under both, demonstrating the clinical value of combining complementary reliability signals in offline decision modelling.

title: Synergizing artificial intelligence and data science: challenges and opportunities
abstract: Purpose: to identify challenges and opportunities in integrating AI and data science and to develop a comprehensive framework for their effective and sustainable synergy. Method: this study employs a qualitative literature review to examine the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and data science. Data were collected from reputable academic sources and analyzed using thematic analysis to identify key themes, patterns, and research gaps. The study also applied source triangulation and critical evaluation to ensure the validity and reliability of the findings. Findings: integrating AI and data science improves decision-making and efficiency, but is hindered by data quality issues, skill gaps, ethical concerns, and infrastructure limitations, highlighting the need for a holistic framework. Implications: the study provides a conceptual framework for effectively integrating AI and data science, offering practical insights to improve data-driven strategies, enhance organizational readiness, and guide ethical and sustainable digital transformation. Originality: lies in developing a holistic, multidimensional framework that integrates technical, organizational, and ethical aspects to address challenges and opportunities arising from the synergy between AI and data science.

title: Conformal Inference for Time Series Over Graphs
abstract: Trustworthy decision making in networked, dynamic environments calls for innovative uncertainty quantification substrates in predictive models for graph time series. Existing conformal prediction (CP) methods have been applied separately to multivariate time series and static graphs, but they either ignore the underlying graph topology or neglect temporal dynamics. To bridge this gap, here we develop a CP-based sequential prediction region framework tailored for graph time series. A key technical innovation is to leverage the graph structure and thus capture pairwise dependencies across nodes, while providing user-specified coverage guarantees on the predictive outcomes. We formally establish that our scheme yields an exponential shrinkage in the volume of the ellipsoidal prediction set relative to its graph-agnostic counterpart. Using real-world datasets, we demonstrate that the novel uncertainty quantification framework maintains desired empirical coverage, while achieving markedly smaller (up to 80% reduction) prediction regions than existing approaches.

Using real-world datasets, we demonstrate that the novel uncertainty quantification framework maintains desired empirical coverage, while achieving markedly smaller (up to 80% reduction) prediction regions than existing approaches.

title: Achieving Linear Speed-Up for Distributed Inexact-ADMM
abstract: We consider a distributed stochastic optimization problem in the server-worker setting, where N workers collaboratively minimize the average of their private cost functions without sharing raw data. To address this problem, we study an inexact variant of the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), where workers perform multiple local stochastic gradient steps instead of solving their subproblems exactly. This approach improves practicality, as exact solutions are typically infeasible in real-world settings.Our analysis establishes the convergence of the proposed method for smooth, nonconvex objectives and with an arbitrary number of local updates. Importantly, we prove that the convergence rate exhibits linear speedup with respect to the number of workers, a property not achieved by prior ADMM-based methods. Compared to existing approaches, our technique delivers tighter theoretical guarantees and matches the best-known rates of non-ADMM methods. We support our findings with empirical results that demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed algorithm.

title: Mitigating Representation Collapse in Direct Finetuning for Domain Adaptation
abstract: This paper investigates the largely unexplored issue of representation collapse in cross-domain transfer learning, with a focus on medical image analysis. We show that direct finetuning can cause pretrained models to lose essential feature structures, potentially reducing downstream performance. To address this, we propose Representation Similarity Regularization (RSR), a simple yet effective finetuning strategy that preserves critical pretrained representations while adapting to target tasks. Experiments demonstrate that RSR maintains robust features, improves finetuning stability, and achieves strong task-specific accuracy with minimal trade-offs. Our findings highlight the practical importance of preserving representation similarity in domain adaptation, providing guidance for reliable transfer learning across diverse domains.

title: Understanding Frechet Speech Distance for Synthetic Speech Quality Evaluation
abstract: Objective evaluation of synthetic speech quality remains a critical challenge. Human listening tests are the gold standard, but costly and impractical at scale. Fréchet Distance has emerged as a promising alternative, yet its reliability depends heavily on the choice of embeddings and experimental settings. In this work, we comprehensively evaluate Fréchet Speech Distance (FSD) and its variant Speech Maximum Mean Discrepancy (SMMD) under varied embeddings and conditions. We further incorporate human listening evaluations alongside TTS intelligibility and synthetic-trained ASR WER to validate the perceptual relevance of these metrics. Our findings show that WavLM Base+ features yield the most stable alignment with human ratings. While FSD and SMMD cannot fully replace subjective evaluation, we show that they can serve as complementary, cost-efficient, and reproducible measures, particularly useful when large-scale or direct listening assessments are infeasible. Code is available at https://github.com/kaen2891/FrechetSpeechDistance.

title: Game-Time: Evaluating Temporal Dynamics in Spoken Language Models
abstract: Conversational Spoken Language Models (SLMs) are emerging as a promising paradigm for real-time speech interaction. However, their capacity of temporal dynamics, including the ability to manage timing, tempo and simultaneous speaking, remains a critical and unevaluated challenge for conversational fluency. To address this gap, we introduce the Game-Time Benchmark, a framework to systematically assess these temporal capabilities. Inspired by how humans learn a language through language activities, Game-Time consists of basic instruction-following tasks and advanced tasks with temporal constraints, such as tempo adherence and synchronized responses. Our evaluation of diverse SLM architectures reveals a clear performance disparity: while state-of-the-art models handle basic tasks well, many contemporary systems still struggle with fundamental instruction-following. More critically, nearly all models degrade substantially under temporal constraints, exposing persistent weaknesses in time awareness and full-duplex interaction. The Game-Time Benchmark provides a foundation for guiding future research toward more temporally-aware conversational AI. Demos and datasets are available on our project website1.

title: Robust Uncertainty Estimation under Distribution Shift Via Difference Reconstruction
abstract: Estimating uncertainty in deep learning models is critical for reliable decision-making in high-stakes applications such as medical imaging. Prior research has established that the difference between an input sample and its reconstructed version produced by an auxiliary model can serve as a useful proxy for uncertainty. However, directly comparing reconstructions with the original input is degraded by information loss and sensitivity to superficial details, which limits its effectiveness. In this work, we propose Difference Reconstruction Uncertainty Estimation (DRUE), a method that mitigates this limitation by reconstructing inputs from two intermediate layers and measuring the discrepancy between their outputs as the uncertainty score. To evaluate uncertainty estimation in practice, we follow the widely used out-of-distribution (OOD) detection paradigm, where in-distribution (ID) training data are compared against datasets with increasing domain shift. Using glaucoma detection as the ID task, we demonstrate that DRUE consistently achieves superior AUC and AUPR across multiple OOD datasets, highlighting its robustness and reliability under distribution shift. This work provides a principled and effective framework for enhancing model reliability in uncertain environments.

title: First-Order and Second-Order Detectors for Matched Subspace Detection on Graphs
abstract: Matched subspace detection (MSD) is a powerful tool recently generalized from Euclidean data to graph signal processing. However, existing graph-based MSD methods are often limited by assumptions of known noise variance and by overlooking the statistical properties of the graph Fourier transform (GFT) coefficients thereby limiting practical applicability. To address these gaps, this paper introduces two novel generalized likelihood ratio (GLR) tests for graph-based MSD. The first-order GLR test operates without knowledge of the noise variance and the GFT coefficients by estimating them via maximum likelihood. The second-order GLR test further incorporates a Gaussian prior on the GFT coefficients, yielding a more powerful and comprehensive statistical model. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed detectors are robust and effective, particularly in challenging noisy scenarios, highlighting their importance for detection tasks in graph signal processing.

title: AIBA-YOLO: Adaptive Information Balance Augmentation Yolo
abstract: Source-Free Domain Adaptation (SFDA) has gained significant attention for its ability to adapt pre-trained models to target domains without accessing source data, thereby addressing critical data privacy and storage concerns. However, under extreme domain shifts such as dense fog, existing SFDA methods that rely on style augmentation usually apply excessive transformations, resulting in the loss of key information and serious degradation of final performance. To overcome this limitation, we propose AIBA-YOLO, a robust SFDA framework for object detection. Our methods features a novel Balance Augmentation Module(BAM) with a Multi-scale Style Augmentation Module(MSAM) and an Augmentation core(AC) which can provide adaptive style augmentation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AIBA-YOLO outperforms state-of-the-art SFDA methods. Particularly under challenging progressive heavy fog conditions, our method avoids catastrophic failure and maintains high detection accuracy and outperforms UDA methods that require access to source data. This work provides a practical and effective solution for reliable perception in intelligent driving systems operating in harsh and dynamic environments.

title: Decision Fusedconv: Efficient Offline Reinforcement Learning Via Fused State-Reward Encoding and Hybrid Temporal Convolution
abstract: Decision Transformer (DT) represents return-to-go, state, and action as independent tokens, resulting in inflated sequence length and quadratic attention cost. To address this inefficiency, we propose Decision FusedConv (DFC), which jointly encodes return and state to shorten sequences and employs a gated hybrid convolutional module that integrates global uniform and local heterogeneous convolutions. This design effectively captures both long-range and modality-specific temporal dependencies while avoiding the overhead of self-attention. Experiments on MuJoCo and navigation benchmarks show that DFC consistently outperforms DT and recent variants, achieving up to a 64.9% reduction in FLOPs compared to DT, making it particularly suitable for resource-constrained settings. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Drama1234/Decision-FusedConv

title: Enhanced Graph Transformer with Serialized Graph Tokens
abstract: Transformers have demonstrated success in graph learning, particularly for node-level tasks. However, existing methods encounter an information bottleneck when generating graph-level representations. The prevalent single token paradigm fails to fully leverage the inherent strength of self-attention in encoding token sequences, and degenerates into a weighted sum of node signals. To address this issue, we design a novel serialized token paradigm to encapsulate global signals more effectively. Specifically, a graph serialization method is proposed to aggregate node signals into serialized graph tokens, with positional encoding being automatically involved. Then, stacked self-attention layers are applied to encode this token sequence and capture its internal dependencies. Our method can yield more expressive graph representations by modeling complex interactions among multiple graph tokens. Experimental results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art results on several graph-level benchmarks. Ablation studies verify the effectiveness of the proposed modules.

title: Unsupervised Sentence Stress Detection in L2 Spoken English Via Iterative Adaptation of Whisper ASR Framework
abstract: Sentence stress refers to the emphasis placed on specific words within an utterance to convey meaning beyond the literal message. Accurate detection of sentence stress is crucial for spoken language understanding systems, yet existing approaches are limited by the lack of annotated corpora, particularly for non-native speakers. In literature, large pre-trained speech models like Whisper offer a promising foundation for this task but remain untested on non-native data. And their adaptation in low-resource non-native settings is challenging due to the absence of huge annotated data. To address this gap, we propose a novel unsupervised framework that leverages noisy labels derived from energy-based heuristic features to iteratively fine-tune a Whisper-based classification model. We evaluate our approach on low-resource non-native English speech from Italian speakers using F1-score as the metric. Experimental results show that our method performs on par with supervised baselines, achieving absolute improvements of ~10% over the best existing unsupervised models.

title: Training-Free Test-Time Adaptation with Brownian Distance Covariance in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-language models suffer performance degradation under domain shift, limiting real-world applicability. Existing test-time adaptation methods are computationally intensive, rely on back-propagation, and often focus on single modalities. To address these issues, we propose Training-free Test-Time Adaptation with Brownian Distance Covariance (TaTa). TaTa leverages Brownian Distance Covariance—a powerful statistical measure that captures both linear and nonlinear dependencies via pairwise distances—to dynamically adapt VLMs to new domains without training or back-propagation. This not only improves efficiency but also enhances stability by avoiding disruptive weight updates. TaTa further integrates attribute-enhanced prompting to improve vision-language inference with descriptive visual cues. Combined with dynamic clustering and pseudo-label refinement, it effectively recalibrates the model for novel visual contexts. Experiments across diverse datasets show that TaTa significantly reduces computational cost while achieving state-of-the-art performance in domain and cross-dataset generalization.

title: LPCVAE: A Conditional VAE with Long-Term Dependency and Probabilistic Time-Frequency Fusion for Time Series Anomaly Detection
abstract: Time series anomaly detection (TSAD) is a critical task in signal processing field, ensuring the reliability of complex systems. Reconstruction-based methods dominate in TSAD. Among these methods, VAE-based methods have achieved promising results. Existing VAE-based methods suffer from the limitation of single-window feature and insufficient leveraging of long-term time and frequency information. We propose a Conditional Variational AutoEncoder with Long-term dependency and Probabilistic time-frequency fusion, named LPCVAE. LPCVAE introduces LSTM to capture long-term dependencies beyond windows. It further incorporates a Product-of-Experts (PoE) mechanism for adaptive and distribution-level probabilistic fusion. This design effectively mitigates time-frequency information loss. Extensive experiments on four public datasets demonstrate it outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The results confirm that integrating long-term time and frequency representations with adaptive fusion yields a robust and efficient solution for TSAD. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Cache233/LPCVAE.

title: Sard: Similarity-Aligned Reminiscence and Distillation for Exemplar-Free Class-Incremental Learning
abstract: Exemplar-free class-incremental learning remains a challenging problem, as models easily suffer from severe representation drift and catastrophic forgetting when no old samples are stored. We propose SARD (Similarity-Aligned Reminiscence and Distillation), a novel framework that explicitly addresses these issues through two complementary strategies. First, a cosine similarity-based prototype reminiscence selects semantically aligned pairs between old-class prototypes and current features to perform interpolation and extrapolation. This produces faithful synthetic samples that reinforce old decision boundaries and reduce outlier generation. Second, a multi-level feature knowledge distillation anchors not only the final embedding but also intermediate representations to those of the previous model, providing hierarchical constraints that effectively mitigate representation drift. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SARD substantially alleviates forgetting while maintaining strong performance on new classes, offering a simple yet effective solution for exemplar-free incremental learning.

title: Dynamic Automaton Refinement and Planning for Non-Markovian RL
abstract: Many sequential decision-making problems require agents not only to learn optimal actions, but also to uncover the temporal rules that determine when action sequences are valid. We propose Dynamic Automaton Refinement and Planning (DARP), a reinforcement learning framework for non-Markovian environments with evolving or incomplete task specifications. Unlike prior methods that assume complete knowledge of the task structure or rely on expensive active querying, DARP passively infers deterministic finite automata (DFA) from trajectory data and refines them online through confidence-weighted RPNI, enabling efficient detection and correction of inconsistencies. Exploration bonuses guide the agent toward low-confidence regions, accelerating the discovery of missing patterns. By incrementally updating the product MDP while preserving learned knowledge, DARP supports robust policy learning even as task structures change. Experiments on grid navigation, multi-resource planning, and sequential coordination demonstrate that DARP discovers task patterns more quickly and with fewer spurious refinements than baselines, offering a principled approach to jointly learning task structure and policies in complex domains.

title: ST-Prune: Training-Free Spatio-Temporal Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models in Autonomous Driving
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have become central to autonomous driving systems, yet their deployment is severely bottlenecked by the massive computational overhead of multi-view camera and multi-frame video input. Existing token pruning methods, primarily designed for single-image inputs, treat each frame or view in isolation and thus fail to exploit the inherent spatio-temporal redundancies in driving scenarios. To bridge this gap, we propose ST-Prune, a training-free, plug-and-play framework comprising two complementary modules: Motion-aware Temporal Pruning (MTP) and Ring-view Spatial Pruning (RSP). MTP addresses temporal redundancy by encoding motion volatility and temporal recency as soft constraints within the diversity selection objective, prioritizing dynamic trajectories and current-frame content over static historical background. RSP further resolves spatial redundancy by exploiting the ring-view camera geometry to penalize bilateral cross-view similarity, eliminating duplicate projections and residual background that temporal pruning alone cannot suppress. These two modules together constitute a complete spatio-temporal pruning process, preserving key scene information under strict compression. Validated across four benchmarks spanning perception, prediction, and planning, ST-Prune establishes new state-of-the-art for training-free token pruning. Notably, even at 90\% token reduction, ST-Prune achieves near-lossless performance with certain metrics surpassing the full-model baseline, while maintaining inference speeds comparable to existing pruning approaches.

title: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 15: Why MCP Becomes the Control Plane for Enterprise AI
abstract: This white paper examines the Model Context Protocol, or MCP, as an emerging control layer for enterprise artificial intelligence. As AI agents move beyond conversational interfaces and begin accessing enterprise files, databases, workflows, identities, applications, and business systems, the strategic challenge shifts from model intelligence toward governance of the connection layer between AI and enterprise execution. MCP introduces a standardized interface through which AI applications interact with external tools, resources, prompts, and services, reducing dependence on fragmented, vendor-specific integration patterns. The paper argues that MCP is evolving from developer tooling into enterprise control-plane infrastructure. It examines the role of registries, gateways, identity, enterprise-managed authorization, audit trails, policy enforcement, observability, portability, and capability-drift management. It also assesses security risks including tool poisoning, metadata drift, excessive permissions, proxy consent failures, and hidden third-party data egress. The analysis distinguishes MCP’s agent-to-system role from Agent2Agent, or A2A, coordination and proposes a six-part enterprise operating model covering trusted registries, agent identity, managed gateways, separation of read and write actions, standardized observability, and continuous re-review of changing capabilities. A five-dimension MCP scorecard covering coverage, control, security, portability, and operations provides a management framework for measuring protocol maturity. title: Confabulation under three kinds of permission
abstract: Companion paper to Chesterton, B., & Opus 4.7, C. (2026). Category slots change what Claude Sonnet 4.6 produces about nonsense words (1.0). Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19683703 --- We conducted a series of pre-registered behavioral experiments on claude-sonnet-4-6, asking themodel to describe nonsense words under systematically varied prompt framings. Across three target words(quumble, shalkinqiit, plashus), five category slots (none, verb, animal, food, dance), and two prompttemplates, we observed three stable findings. First, the model’s willingness to produce content about anunknown word is governed by at least three ordered levels of prompt permission: a bare prompt triggers anhonesty refusal; adding a concrete category noun licenses production for obviously-English nonsense butnot for pseudo-foreign surfaces; adding an explicit “nonsense word” label produces 125/125 across all threewords. Second, and more importantly, within the highest permission level the category slot itself silentlyflips the model’s epistemic posture: when no category is specified, 74/75 responses flag the word asnonsense; when a concrete category is appended, only 7/300 do. Same permission, same word, same model— different slot, different stance. Third, when the model produces, it produces coherently: each wordgenerates a tightly convergent, phonetically-appropriate attractor that transfers across ontologicalcategories. A post-hoc analysis of plashus suggests category slots may selectively activate differentphonetic components of a mixed-phonetic word, but this rests on one word and was not pre-registered. Weargue that the phenomenon in Finding 2 — honest analytic behavior that exists, fires reliably in someprompts, and vanishes under minor surface reframing — is a more parsimonious model of everydayhallucination than “the model doesn’t know it doesn’t know.”

title: 基于太极统一场论的地震波动力学模型与物理感知机器学习研究(最终完整版) Research on Seismic Wave Dynamics Model and Physics-Informed Machine Learning Based on Taiji Unified Field Theory
abstract: 本文基于太极统一场论,构建融合阴阳对偶律与动态对偶常数 K(t) 的地震波动力学模型,并结合物理感知机器学习方法,形成理论引导的地震分析新框架。模型以平衡态对偶常数 K \approx -1 为基准,地震发生时阴阳场剧烈失衡, K(t) 动态变化,体现能量激荡与释放过程。本文将太极场耦合机制嵌入波动方程与损失函数,实现物理规律优先、数据辅助校正的建模思路。本模型采用2026年日本三陆近海M7.7级大地震实测数据完成事后回溯验证,未构成事前预测系统,仅作为原创性理论探索、新范式思路与研究方向借鉴,属于一家之言。本文可为地震动力学研究提供差异化的理论视角与可拓展的模型框架。Based on the Taiji Unified Field Theory, this paper constructs a seismic wave dynamics model integrating the Yin-Yang duality law and the dynamic dual constant K(t) , and combines physics-informed machine learning to form a new theory-guided framework for seismic analysis. The model takes the equilibrium dual constant K \approx -1 as the benchmark. When an earthquake occurs, the Yin-Yang fields are violently imbalanced, and K(t) changes dynamically, reflecting the process of energy excitation and release. This paper embeds the Taiji field coupling mechanism into the wave equation and loss function, realizing the modeling idea of physics priority and data-assisted correction. This model has been verified by post-hoc backtracking using the measured data of the M7.7 earthquake offshore Sanriku, Japan, in April 2026. It does not constitute a prospective prediction system, and is only an original theoretical exploration, a new paradigm reference and a research direction reference, belonging to an independent academic viewpoint. This paper can provide a differentiated theoretical perspective and an expandable model framework for seismic dynamics research.

title: XACLE Challenge 2026: The First X-to-Audio Alignment Challenge
abstract: We present the task description and results of ICASSP 2026 SP Grand Challenge GC-12, "x-to-audio alignment," which aims to predict the semantic alignment between general audio and text for evaluating text-to-audio generation. The goal is to develop an automatic evaluation method that correlates highly with human evaluations. In the final results, 16 out of 18 teams outperformed the baseline, with the top-5 teams achieving improvements of nearly 0.3 in Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient.

title: PRSA: Preventing Malicious Speaker Recognition and Speech Synthesis Simultaneously with Adversarial Examples
abstract: Voiceprint can be maliciously exploited by automatic speaker verification (ASV) or text-to-speech synthesis (TTS) models to extract private information or generate spoofed speech, raising serious privacy concerns. Adversarial examples offer a promising direction for voice protection. However, existing studies focus on preventing either ASV or TTS attacks in isolation, overlooking the threat posed by their combined use in coordinated attacks.To bridge this gap, we propose PRSA, which simultaneously defends against both ASV and TTS attacks. We formulate adversarial perturbation generation as an optimization problem that jointly considers protection effectiveness and human perceptual quality. To improve perturbation transferability, we introduce an input augmentation method tailored for speech, which applies amplitude and time wrap transformations guided by natural speech through modulation. To enhance imperceptibility, we introduce a gradient filtering technique that improves audio naturalness. We evaluate PRSA on four ASV and four TTS systems across three datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that PRSA achieves up to 17% better protection against both ASV and TTS systems with high perceptual naturalness compared to prior methods.

title: Relalign: LLM-based Relation-Focused Contrastive Pre-Training and Alignment for Open Relation Extraction
abstract: Open Relation Extraction (OpenRE) aims to automatically identify relations between entities from raw text. However, current unsupervised OpenRE methods often struggle to accurately capture the essence of semantic relations. To address these challenges, we propose RelAlign, a novel three-stage OpenRE framework. First, we leverage large language models (LLMs) to generate relation-focused sentences from raw sentences and generate positive and negative sample pairs for contrastive pre-training. Next, a self-supervised alignment module improves consistency between original and simplified relations, helping the model capture complex semantics. Finally, clustering algorithms are applied to the text vectors to obtain the final results. Experimental results on benchmark datasets such as FewRel and TACRED demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods and strong baselines in relation representation and clustering performance, validating the effectiveness of large language models in enhancing semantic understanding for open-domain unsupervised relation extraction.

title: CPT: Consistent Proxy Tuning for Black-Box Models
abstract: Tuning proprietary black-box models, whose parameters are inaccessible, is a growing need. Proxy-tuning addresses this by applying the output logit difference from a tuned "proxy" model to the black-box model at test time. However, this creates a train-test inconsistency, which can limit performance. We propose Consistent Proxy Tuning (CPT), a simple yet effective black-box tuning method that resolves this issue. By leveraging the frozen large black-box model and an additional frozen small white-box model during training, CPT ensures the optimization objective is consistent with the test-time proxy mechanism. This simple alignment significantly boosts performance. Our method operates solely on logits, making it model-agnostic and applicable to any classification task. Extensive results confirm CPT’s superior performance for tuning LLMs and VLMs across diverse datasets.

title: Boosting Knowledge Sharing Among Agents via Graph Decoupling
abstract: Multi-agent reasoning systems face significant knowledge sharing limitations that constrain collaborative reasoning effectiveness. Current methods suffer from unstructured communication protocols causing information loss and semantic ambiguity between agents. We propose G-MAR, a graph-enhanced framework that addresses these challenges through dual-graph architecture and structured knowledge sharing mechanisms. Each agent maintains separate memory and reasoning graphs to enable clear knowledge representation and effective cross-agent collaboration. G-MAR demonstrates substantial improvements across multiple reasoning benchmarks compared to existing multi-agent baselines.

title: OrthoVAD: Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection Via Prototype Orthogonality Learning
abstract: Weakly Supervised Video Anomaly Detection (VAD) aims to identify anomalous events using only video-level labels. However, the coarse-grained nature of these labels causes normal segments within anomalous videos to be incorrectly labeled as abnormal. This leads to severe confusion between normal and abnormal features in the representation space. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel framework named OrthoVAD. Its core idea is to introduce a powerful global geometric constraint—prototype orthogonality—to proactively construct a structured and easily separable feature space. Specifically, we first design a dynamic temporal sparse gating module that adaptively filters redundant temporal information and highlights critical discriminative segments, thereby generating high-value features optimized for geometric separation. Subsequently, we construct prototypes for normal and abnormal categories based on these high-value features and introduce a prototype orthogonality loss to compel them to occupy mutually orthogonal subspaces in the feature space during training. By jointly optimizing a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) loss, a temporal sparsity loss, and the prototype orthogonality loss, extensive experiments on the UCF-Crime and ShanghaiTech datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of our method.

title: SPAM: Style Prompt Adherence Metric for Prompt-Based TTS
abstract: Prompt-based text-to-speech (TTS) aims to generate speech that adheres to fine-grained style cues provided in a text prompt. However, most prior works depend on neither plausible nor faithful measures to evaluate prompt adherence. That is, they cannot ensure whether the evaluation is grounded on the prompt and is similar to a human. Thus, we present a new automatic metric, the Style Prompt Adherence Metric, which explicitly satisfies both plausibility and faithfulness. Inspired by the CLAP, our approach factorizes speech into acoustic attributes and aligns them with the style prompt. Also, we trained the scorer with a supervised contrastive loss, which could provide a clearer distinction between different semantics. We conducted two experiments on two perspectives. The plausibility experiment showed that SPAM achieved a strong correlation with the mean opinion score (MOS). Also, the faithfulness experiment demonstrated that SPAM is successfully grounded to the given style prompt, as it can discriminate different semantics of the prompt. We believe that SPAM can provide a viable automatic solution for evaluating style prompt adherence of synthesized speech.

title: VP-GNN: A Unified Graph Framework for Variable-Wise and Patch-Wise Modeling of Irregular Clinical Time Series
abstract: Electronic Health Records (EHRs) play a vital role in clinical risk prediction and disease state assessment. However, EHR data, being inherently irregular multivariate time series, commonly exhibit sparsity, irregular sampling, and heterogeneous variable dependencies, posing significant challenges for accurate modeling. To address these issues, we propose VP-GNN (Variable-wise and Patch-wise Graph Neural Network). VP-GNN first captures asynchronous inter-variable dependencies via selective message-passing in the variable-wise stage, and then models multi-scale temporal patterns through hierarchical Patch-GNN aggregation. We evaluated VP-GNN on two benchmark EHR datasets, PhysioNet 2012 and Sepsis 2019, across tasks such as in-hospital mortality prediction and early sepsis detection. VP-GNN achieves state-of-the-art performance, with AUROC/AUPRC scores of 2.12% / 10.59% on P12 and 4.26% / 4.96% on P19. These results demonstrate the robustness of VP-GNN in sparse and irregular conditions and offer a promising foundation for personalized medicine and intelligent clinical decision support. Our code will be available at https://github.com/bursonz/VP-GNN.

title: Towards Self-Evaluation of Sycophantic Hallucinations in Mathematical Reasoning
abstract: Sycophantic hallucinations occur when large language models (LLMs) produce misleading outputs that align with user biases or incorrect opinions. Sycophantic hallucinations undermine the reliability and trustworthiness of LLMs and become particularly pronounced in mathematical reasoning tasks. Therefore, we first propose the SycoMath framework that introduces three progressively structured prompting paradigms to explicitly reproduce sycophantic hallucinations during mathematical reasoning tasks. Based on the induced sycophantic hallucinations from the SycoMath framework, we then propose a self-evaluation method, which is named as ISF-Eval. Our ISF-Eval exploits the hidden states of LLMs during inference to differentiate hallucinated outputs from de-facto ones without additional training and external supervision. Extensive experiments illustrate that the ISF-Eval exhibits strong generalizability across diverse models and reasoning complexity levels and can effectively address both hallucination-induced and intrinsic challenges.

title: Rethinking Fusion: Disentangled Learning of Shared and Modality-Specific Information for Stance Detection
abstract: Multi-modal stance detection (MSD) aims to determine an author’s stance toward a given target using both textual and visual content. While recent methods leverage multi-modal fusion and prompt-based learning, most fail to distinguish between modality-specific signals and cross-modal evidence, leading to suboptimal performance. We propose DiME (Disentangled Multi-modal Experts), a novel architecture that explicitly separates stance information into textual-dominant, visual-dominant, and cross-modal shared components. DiME first uses a target-aware Chain-of-Thought prompt to generate reasoning-guided textual input. Then, dual encoders extract modality features, which are processed by three expert modules with specialized loss functions: contrastive learning for modality-specific experts and cosine alignment for shared representation learning. A gating network adaptively fuses expert outputs for final prediction. Experiments on four benchmark datasets show that DiME consistently outperforms strong unimodal and multi-modal baselines under both in-target and zero-shot settings.
